blocks.text: Sadi Carnot in 1824 described an ideal engine using only isothermal and adiabatic processes. He showed that a heat engine operating in an ideal reversible cycle between two heat reservoirs at different temperatures would be the most efficient engine. A Carnot cycle using an ideal gas as the working substance is shown on a PV diagram (Fig. 6.9); it consists of four steps:

blocks.alt: A P-V graph of the Carnot cycle A to B to C to D to A, with the enclosed region shaded. A to B is a green curve labelled Isotherm, B to C a steeper magenta curve labelled Adiabat, C to D a green Isotherm back to the left and D to A a magenta Adiabat up to A; arrows show the direction. Dashed lines drop from A, D, B and C to V1, V4, V2 and V3.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.9: Carnot cycle on a PV diagram (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.9).

items: The gas is allowed to expand isothermally at temperature T1, absorbing heat Q1 from the hot reservoir; the process is represented by the curve AB.
The gas is then allowed to expand adiabatically until its temperature drops to T2; the curve BC.
The gas at this stage is compressed isothermally at temperature T2, rejecting heat Q2 to the cold reservoir; the curve CD.
Finally the gas is compressed adiabatically to restore its initial state at temperature T1; the curve DA.

blocks.text: Thermal and mechanical equilibrium is maintained all the time, so that each process is perfectly reversible. As the working substance returns to the initial state there is no change in its internal energy, delta U = 0. The net work done during one cycle equals the area enclosed by the path ABCDA of the PV diagram; it can also be estimated from the net heat delta Q absorbed in one cycle: Q = Q1 - Q2. From the first law Q = delta U + W, or W = Q1 - Q2 (since delta U = 0).

blocks.title: Efficiency of a heat engine
blocks.text: The efficiency eta of the heat engine is defined as eta = output (work) / input (energy), thus eta = (Q1 - Q2)/Q1 ... (6.6). The energy transfer in an isothermal expansion or compression turns out to be proportional to the kelvin temperature, so Q1 and Q2 are proportional to the kelvin temperatures T1 and T2, and hence eta = (T1 - T2)/T1 = 1 - T2/T1 ... (6.7). The efficiency is usually taken as a percentage: percentage efficiency = (1 - T2/T1) x 100.

Thus the efficiency of a Carnot engine depends on the temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs; it is independent of the nature of the working substance. The larger the temperature difference of the two reservoirs, the greater the efficiency; but it can never be one or 100% unless the cold reservoir is at absolute zero (T2 = 0 K). Such reservoirs are not available, so the maximum efficiency is always less than one. Nevertheless the Carnot cycle establishes an upper limit on the efficiency of all heat engines; no practical heat engine can be perfectly reversible and energy dissipation is inevitable. A waterfall driving a wheel is an analogy for the heat engine (Interesting Information).

blocks.title: Carnot's theorem
blocks.text: No heat engine can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same two temperatures. The theorem can be extended to state that all Carnot engines operating between the same two temperatures have the same efficiency, irrespective of the nature of the working substance.

In most practical cases the cold reservoir is near room temperature, so the efficiency can only be increased by raising the temperature of the hot reservoir. All real heat engines are less efficient than the Carnot engine due to friction and other heat losses.

blocks.title: Example 6.3
blocks.text: The turbine in a steam power plant takes steam from a boiler at 427 degrees C and exhausts into a low-temperature reservoir at 77 degrees C. What is the maximum possible efficiency? Solution: the maximum efficiency for any engine operating between temperatures T1 and T2 is eta = ((T1 - T2)/T1) x 100, where T1 = 427 + 273 = 700 K and T2 = 77 + 273 = 350 K. So (T1 - T2)/T1 = (700 K - 350 K)/700 K = 350 K/700 K = 1/2 = 0.5, or eta = 0.5 x 100 = 50%.
